ut_confluence_the_2.blurb: A busy sandstone crag in Zion National Park, set above the Zion-Mount Carmel Highway near Springdale. Most of the twenty routes are single-pitch traditional lines, with a couple of bolted sport lines, plus a few longer multi-pitch outings. Grades start around 5.6 and run to 5.11, with the bulk in the 5.10 and 5.11 range, so strong leaders have the most to chase while there is a thin set of easier warm-ups. The wall takes strong afternoon sun and is cooler early in the day. Views stretch over the canyon mouth and the town below. The rock is fragile when damp, so let it dry fully before pulling on it.

ut_cliff_lake.blurb: A high-elevation quartzite crag in the western Uinta Mountains, above a quiet alpine lake at roughly 10,000 feet. The cliff is a south-facing band about 90 feet tall and a hundred yards across, so it warms up early and makes a pleasant summer escape from valley heat. Routes are short single pitches, a mix of bolted lines and traditional climbs, mostly between 5.6 and 5.10 with a few harder ones. A small rack is useful even on the bolted lines. The setting is scenic, there is a sheltered alcove if a storm rolls in, and the wall is big enough for more than one party.

ut_umwa_boulder.blurb: A single large sandstone boulder in the Right Fork canyon of Joe's Valley, in central Utah, with problems on every side of it. It holds about twenty problems that cover a wide spread, from very easy up to V8, though the middle band around V3 to V5 has the most traffic and the best-known classics. Because the boulder sits at the pull-off, there is almost no walking, which makes it an easy first or last stop of the day. The canyon is chilly in the early hours. Sandstone here loses strength when wet, so give it a few dry days after any precipitation.

vt_main_cliff_2.blurb: A steep dolomite cliff rising over Lake Champlain on Lone Rock Point, just north of Burlington. This is a specialist's wall: roughly two dozen bolted routes, nearly all of them hard, with the weight of the grades at 5.13 and 5.14 and only a few lines easier than 5.12. Expect overhanging, technical face climbing with plenty of variations. Most routes face west and catch the sun from midday into the evening. Many lines are best clipped with a stick clip at the start. It is a distinctive New England experience, and quite unlike the schist found elsewhere in the state.

vt_e_lower_tier.blurb: A sector of the Upper West cliffs in Bolton, Vermont, on schist reached from Bolton Notch Road. About two dozen routes, mostly bolted with a handful of traditional lines, including a couple of easy corners and one two-pitch route. The grades run from 5.7 to 5.12, but the sweet spot is the 5.10 and 5.11 sport climbing, with a few 5.9s to warm up on. The rock is varied here, from very solid to a bit loose. Some lines dry quickly after rain while others seep for longer, so conditions matter. It sits a hike of roughly twenty minutes or more into the woods.

vt_asteroid_the.blurb: A cluster of schist boulders near the height of land in Smugglers' Notch, Vermont, in the Top of the Notch zone. About two dozen problems, none of them beginner terrain: the easiest are around V3, most of the meat sits between V4 and V8, and a few lines reach into double digits. Boomerang and Pulled Pork are the most popular. The boulder stands up the slope from the Backyard Boulder, so expect a short uphill walk through the trees. Schist gets slick when it is hot or damp, so cool, dry days work best. Bring several pads.

vt_b_f_b.blurb: A steep bouldering zone at the highest point of Smugglers' Notch in Vermont, across the road from the Shark Fin boulder, on schist. Roughly two dozen problems, and it is known for some of the hardest boulder lines in the state: many are V10 and up, with a few reaching V13 and V14. There are still a handful of moderate options, including an elegant high arete at V1 that is a draw for anyone climbing lower grades. Landings and height deserve a careful look. Schist turns slippery in heat and after rain, so wait for dry conditions.
